articles.title: Brazil’s US$23bn green hydrogen pipeline awaits offtake deals, financing - BNamericas
articles.summary: Brazil’s US$23bn green hydrogen pipeline awaits offtake deals, financing  BNamericas
articles.full_text:
Members of Brazil’s green hydrogen industry association ABIHV have more than R$115bn (US$23.1bn) in projects with a final investment decision (FID) expected by 2030, but the ventures still depend on offtake and/or financing agreements, licensing and infrastructure to move forward.
The portfolio of the association’s members comprises 10.4 GW of electrolysis capacity, with projects at different stages of development, according to Fernanda Delgado, CEO of ABIHV.
“The implementation of the projects should take place in stages, with the schedules subject to final investment decisions (FIDs) and the completion of the development phases,” he told BNamericas.
Among the projects with operation dates announced by the developers, Qair plans to start a first 20 MW phase of the Fraternité project in 2028, while FRV estimates that H2 Cumbuco will come online by 2030.
Read more: CELA: Cost of green hydrogen should drop even further in Brazil
The outlook for the sector also depends on the evolution of international demand and the ability to structure long-term contracts, especially for projects aimed at exports.
Europe and demand for green hydrogen
The reprioritization of European investments, with greater attention to energy security and military capacity, may affect the pace of development of Brazilian projects, especially those intended for export.
"The competition for public resources and the uncertainties about European demand may prolong the negotiation of purchase contracts and investment decisions," Delgado told BNamericas.
She pointed out that, although Europe maintains decarbonization policies that include renewable hydrogen and its imports, these guidelines still need to translate into contracts and financing conditions.
"Brazil brings together significant advantages in the supply of renewable energy, but the competitiveness of the projects also depends on infrastructure, cost of capital, logistics, and access to markets," emphasized Delgado.
In light of this, ABIHV considers it important to develop domestic demand, expanding marketing possibilities and offering greater support for investments.
An opportunity for Brazilian producers is in the second round of H2Global. The South America and Oceania Lot (South American & Oceanian Lot, SAL) has already been launched, and the registration deadline for interested parties has closed. The process is now in the evaluation and contracting phase of the proposals.
The lot has a minimum budget of €587 million and includes three products: renewable hydrogen, renewable ammonia, and renewable methanol. The products must meet the European criteria for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO).
In H2Global’s first renewable ammonia tender, no Brazilian project was selected. The winner was Fertiglobe, with production in Egypt. In this mechanism, Hintco acts as an intermediary buyer, entering into long-term contracts with producers and reselling the products to the European market.
Delgado stressed that H2Global must be distinguished from the auctions already carried out by the European Hydrogen Bank, which support production in the European Economic Area. The bank’s international pillar, focused on imports, remains under development.
Different development models
The green hydrogen projects in operation or in pilot phase in Brazil illustrate different paths to develop the market, according to the executive.
White Martins already produces certified green hydrogen on an industrial scale in Pernambuco and supplies gases for industrial applications. In Jacareí, São Paulo, the company has announced that it will serve glass manufacturer Cebrace and other industrial consumers.
“This connection with defined applications and clients favors the commercial structuring of investments,” said Delgado.
Neoenergia, in turn, developed a pilot plant focused on the production and supply of hydrogen for mobility, with resources from the Research, Development and Innovation Program regulated by the National Electric Energy Agency (Aneel).
In this case, the research funding and the goal of technological demonstration help explain the implementation of the unit.
"Large-scale projects, especially those intended for export, need to coordinate larger volumes of purchasing, financing, and infrastructure, which makes their implementation more complex," noted the CEO of ABIHV.
Access to the network is decisive
Access to the basic transmission grid remains among the determining factors for the viability of green hydrogen projects. The connection requires an assessment of available capacity, deadlines, technical requirements, and financial guarantees.
The National Policy for Access to the Transmission System (PNAST), established by Decree No. 12.772/2025, created access seasons to organize requests and capacity allocation. The National Electric System Operator (ONS) has already announced the end of the first season, which represents progress in the implementation of the model.
The effects of the policy on hydrogen projects, however, need to be assessed based on concrete results in terms of access, the costs involved, and the compatibility between the transmission expansion schedules and those of the projects.
"There may be competition with data centers when projects seek connection in regions or locations with limited capacity," warned Delgado.
Read also: Data centers secure access to the power grid in São Paulo
For ABIHV, transmission planning needs to be coordinated with the needs of different consumers, in order to enable the development of digital infrastructure and the green hydrogen industry with safety and predictability.
(The original version of this content was written in Portuguese)

articles.title: Singapore plans five gas-fired power plants, second LNG terminal to lift capacity 26% by early 2030s - Pipeline and Gas Journal
articles.summary: Singapore plans five gas-fired power plants, second LNG terminal to lift capacity 26% by early 2030s  Pipeline and Gas Journal
articles.full_text:
Singapore to add five gas-fired power plants by 2032 and a second LNG terminal at Jurong Port, lifting power capacity 26% as data center demand grows.
(P&GJ) — Singapore will build five new gas-fired power plants to raise its electricity generation capacity by about 26% from roughly 12 gigawatts (GW) early next decade, Tan See Leng, minister for energy, trade and industry, said Monday.
Speaking at the Singapore International Energy Week conference, Tan said the projects are part of the Energy Market Authority's five-year plan to meet growing demand and strengthen the city-state's energy resilience. The authority is evaluating proposals for the plants, which are expected to begin operating by 2032, and will issue further requests for proposals over the next five years if demand growth remains strong.
Peak demand reached 8.6 GW as of August 2026 and could rise to between 9.9 GW and 13 GW by 2031, driven by semiconductor manufacturing, data centers and electric vehicles. Natural gas supplies about 95% of Singapore's electricity.
Singapore will expand its liquefied natural gas (LNG) regasification capacity to 15 MMtpy from 10 MMtpy when a second terminal at Jurong Port begins operating by 2030.
The government expects to invest up to $4.15 billion (S$5.3 billion) in its power grid from 2025 to 2029, including seven new transmission substations by 2031, compared with four in the previous five years.
Subsea surveys began this month for a second power interconnector with Peninsular Malaysia, which would add up to 2 GW of capacity by 2030 alongside the existing 1 GW link.
Singapore also plans to increase energy storage capacity to just over 1 gigawatt-hour by 2030 from about 350 megawatt-hours. Solar capacity stands at 2.3 GWp, with targets of 3 GWp by 2030 and 4 GWp by 2035.

Agricultural train wreck and the 2027 global food crisis
Richard Mills examines how rising fertilizer and diesel costs, a Super El Nino and the Iran war are setting up a global food crisis in 2027.
Investorideas.com (www.investorideas.com) Article from Richard Mills.
The FAO Food Price Index rose for a third consecutive month in September 2026, marking a 1.5% increase from August and reaching its highest level since November 2022.
Prices are up 5.8% compared to September 2025.
Food prices are climbing due to a combination of:
- Rising production costs. Higher oil and diesel prices increase the cost of running farm machinery and transporting goods. Imported fertilizers and materials like steel for cans cost more due to trade tariffs.
- Reduced agricultural labor pools have driven up wages and harvesting expenses.
- Extreme weather. Droughts, floods, and unseasonal freezes have hurt crop yields globally.
- Supply chain disruptions. Multi-year droughts forced farmers to shrink cattle herds, pushing beef prices to record highs. Regional conflicts and port delays slow down transit times for fresh food.
- Corporate profit margins. A small number of massive corporations control major parts of the food supply chain, limiting price competition. Many large food companies raised prices during inflation spikes to protect or expand their profit margins.
When grocery budgets are squeezed, families protect their immediate hunger by buying cheap, calorie-dense starchy staples (like rice, maize or bread) while cutting out expensive, nutrient-dense foods (like meat, dairy, vegetables and fruit).
Families in developing nations spend 50% to 100% of their income on food (compared to 12%-30% in wealthier countries). Historically, sharp food price spikes directly trigger civil unrest, food riots, and political upheavals. When local agricultural systems collapse from high input costs or climate stress, families are forced to displace and migrate to survive.
According to the latest UN Hunger Hotspots Report and updates from the World Food Program (WFP), 266 million people globally are facing acute, crisis-level hunger.
The primary driver of hunger is that 2.7 billion people simply cannot afford a healthy diet. This is because food is treated as a global commodity, meaning it flows to where the profit is, not where the hunger is.
A major reason food prices spike unpredictably is because of financial speculation. Investment banks and hedge funds are buying and selling food contracts strictly to make a profit on price movements.
Fertilizer and farming
US fertilizer prices continued climbing during the week of Oct. 12-16, with nitrogen products recording the strongest monthly increases as farmers faced renewed pressure on production costs. Retail market figures released Oct. 21 showed UAN32 rising to $486 per ton, UAN28 reaching $441 and anhydrous ammonia climbing to $987. The increases matter because nitrogen is a major variable expense in corn production, and higher replacement costs could influence fertilizer purchases, crop budgets and planting decisions heading into 2027.
The latest market figures show a broad-based increase rather than an isolated nitrogen price adjustment. Seven of eight major fertilizer products became more expensive over the preceding month, while liquid starter fertilizer 10-34-0 was the only category to decline. UAN32 recorded a 6% monthly increase, while UAN28 and anhydrous ammonia each rose approximately 5%. The upward movement comes as agricultural producers evaluate whether expected commodity revenue can absorb another round of input inflation without further weakening operating margins. (AgroLatam)
Agricultural fertilizers face an extended, painful pricing plateau.
A dramatic divide is emerging between the industrial sector and the agricultural supply chain.
According to a report by consultancy firm CRU released at London Metal Exchange (LME) Week, sulfuric acid prices will extend their decline in 2027. Prices delivered to top copper producers like Chile are projected to plummet to $215 a metric ton by Q4 2027, down from an extreme, war-driven record high of $451 earlier this year.
Note that while processed acid is falling, raw elemental sulfur remains critically bottlenecked at the Strait of Hormuz, maintaining a deep divergence between industrial chemical markets and agricultural inputs.
Roughly half of the global sulfur supply is stuck behind the Strait of Hormuz or locked in Russia. This raw sulfur shortage has sent input costs skyrocketing by 130%, prompting China to implement export bans.
North Dakota State University projections indicate that fertilizer prices will plateau at highly elevated levels well above pre-war averages through 2028. For 2027, diammonium phosphate (DAP) is projected to average $666/ton (up from traditional baselines but down from its $901 peaks), while urea is expected to stabilize near $496/ton.
Josh Linville, vice president of fertilizer at StoneX Group, says tight nitrogen supplies, rising demand and global disruptions to sulfur supplies are keeping pressure on fertilizer markets even if tensions in the Strait of Hormuz ease.
As reported by AgWeb Farm Journal:
          "Even if we solve the Strait of Hormuz right now and everything went back to normal - vessel traffic, peace, all those fun things - I think we're still talking about this in spring 2027," Linville says. "I don't think farmers are getting out of this."
Fertilizer costs are already climbing as farmers prepare for the 2027 growing season. University of Illinois researchers report that diammonium phosphate (DAP) prices have risen from about $700 per ton early in 2026 to around $850 per ton, while sulfur prices have surged more than 130% since the beginning of the year. Researchers warn continued sulfur supply disruptions could push phosphate fertilizer costs higher.
AgroLatam agrees that rising fertilizer prices, tight nitrogen supplies and global trade disruptions threaten US farm margins as growers prepare for the 2027 planting season.
          U.S. farmers are facing mounting fertilizer supply risks as of October 21, 2026, with industry analysts warning that disruptions in global nitrogen, phosphate and sulfur markets could extend into spring 2027. The outlook matters because producers across the Corn Belt are already preparing crop budgets and securing inputs for next season. Even if shipping conditions improve in the Strait of Hormuz, depleted inventories and manufacturing constraints could keep fertilizer prices elevated, creating another financial challenge for American agriculture.
The pressure is becoming increasingly visible in fertilizer markets. Research published by the University of Illinois' farmdoc daily in August showed diammonium phosphate (DAP) prices climbing from approximately $700 to $850 per ton during 2026, an increase of more than 20%. Sulfur prices rose more than 130% from the beginning of the year, adding substantial pressure to phosphate production costs. These increases are particularly concerning for corn producers, whose fertilizer requirements make them more exposed to changes in nitrogen and phosphate prices.
The financial consequences extend well beyond individual fertilizer purchases. In its September 2026 farm income outlook, the USDA projected total U.S. agricultural production expenses of $492.8 billion for 2026, up 4.5% from the previous year. Spending on fertilizer, lime and soil conditioners was expected to increase by $5.3 billion, or 15.3%. Those figures underscore how rising input costs can weaken farm profitability even when commodity prices provide some revenue support, especially for producers operating with limited working capital.
Diesel
US diesel prices have nearly doubled this year, reaching $6.27 a gallon for the week of Oct. 19.
Most people have no idea how fragile and fuel-dependent the modern food supply really is. Diesel runs the tractors that plow the fields. It runs the harvesters that bring in the crops. It runs the refrigerated trucks that move produce from farm to distribution center. It runs the trains that carry grain across continents. It runs the ships that haul food between nations. Every single link in the food chain depends on diesel - and there is no substitute at scale.
This is the reality that the climate alarmists and the energy transition fantasists refuse to acknowledge. You cannot run a modern agricultural system on solar panels and wind turbines. You cannot harvest wheat with an electric combine that runs for six hours before needing a charge. The scale of energy required to feed eight billion people is staggering, and the vast majority of it comes from fossil fuels. When diesel becomes scarce or unaffordable, the entire system seizes up.
Worse still, fertilizer production is also tied to energy - specifically natural gas. As energy costs spike, fertilizer production becomes unprofitable. As fertilizer production declines, farmers cannot afford to fertilize their fields. As fertilization declines, yields collapse. This is a chain reaction that cannot be stopped once it begins. As I wrote in a prior article, 'This is not a drought or a plague - it is a man-made catastrophe'. The destruction of affordable energy is the quickest path to starvation hell. (Natural News)
Super El Nino
The intensifying 2026-27 "Super El Nino" is projected by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to be one of the most destructive climate events in 50 years, severely disrupting agriculture.
WMO forecasts a near-100% likelihood that El Nino will persist through February 2027 and could be the strongest ever, raising risks of extreme weather into next year. Only three very strong or Super El Ninos have been recorded since 1950. The last Super El Nino occurred in 2015-16.

articles.title: The Rise of the Electrostate: Why Protectionism Alone Cannot Close the Critical Minerals Gap - IndraStra Global
articles.summary: The Rise of the Electrostate: Why Protectionism Alone Cannot Close the Critical Minerals Gap  IndraStra Global
articles.full_text:
Why protectionism cannot close the critical minerals gap, and how refining, industrial investment & supply-chain diversification reshape global power.
An average that folds every refinery into one number hides the stage at which dependence actually forms, so the chain has to be separated into reserves, mining, refining, intermediate materials and finished products. Mining is slowly diversifying. The IEA's full report finds that the top three producing countries supply around 76% of global mine output, projected to ease to 73% by 2035. Refining is "considerably starker": China holds just under 50% of global copper refining capacity, 70% of lithium refining, 75% of cobalt refining, 85% of magnet rare earth separation and over 90% of battery-grade graphite production. Rare earths, a family of distinct elements with separate markets, can be controlled one element at a time.
Placing the IEA's mining and processing figures for six minerals side by side reveals the distance between the two stages, and how differently each is expected to move by 2035.
| Mineral | Mining picture (IEA, 2025) | China's share of refining or processing (IEA, 2025) | IEA base-case direction to 2035 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Lithium | Australia, Chile and China together about 75% | 70% of refining | Top-three mining share falls below 70% | 
| Graphite | China about 80% of mined natural graphite | 94% of battery-grade supply | China's mined share 53%; battery-grade share 91% | 
| Magnet rare earths | China around 60% of mined supply | 85% of separation, down from 90% in 2024 | Mining 55%; separation 73% | 
| Cobalt | Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) under export quotas since October 2025 | 75% of refining | Supply gap above 25% in 2035 | 
| Nickel | Indonesia's share rising above 70% | Indonesia is the top refiner | Concentration keeps increasing | 
| Copper | Latin America about 40% of mining | Just under 50% of refining capacity | Supply deficit of about 25% in 2035 | 
If the table locates concentration in processing, the obvious follow-up is why a refinery cannot simply be built elsewhere once tariffs make imports dearer. The IEA's answer is that refining capacity "remains closely linked to established chemical processing infrastructure, accumulated technical expertise and proximity to downstream manufacturing." Capital costs for refining projects are 20% to over 150% higher outside the dominant supplier. That ecosystem of equipment, chemists, supplier density and scale does not respond quickly to import prices. A process proven in a pilot plant is not yet commercial supply: it must deliver volume, quality and consistency at competitive cost, and buyers must qualify the material first, one of the switching costs the IEA lists with testing and certification. Rare earth equipment made outside China can cost 5 to 12 times more and take two to three times longer to arrive, from manufacturers that "have not secured long-term established customers."
Changing the battery recipe looks like a way around the refinery problem, but the IEA's chemistry data show that it relocates exposure without removing it. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) accounted for 55% of global electric vehicle (EV) batteries sold in 2025, and LFP packs were more than 40% cheaper on average per kilowatt-hour than lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) packs. Choosing LFP sheds the need for cobalt and nickel, but both chemistries still need lithium and graphite anodes, and China produced 98% of LFP cathode materials in 2025, two-thirds of nickel-based cathode material and more than 90% of anode material. Its October 2025 battery controls, now suspended, named LFP cathode materials among their targets.
Neither a new refinery nor a new chemistry escapes China's processing base quickly, and the export-control notices issued in Beijing since late 2024 showed what that concentration can be used for. The Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM; 中华人民共和国商务部) issued Announcement No. 46 of 2024 on December 3, 2024, banning dual-use exports to US military users and stating that gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials would in principle not be licensed for the United States. On April 4, 2025, MOFCOM and the General Administration of Customs placed seven medium and heavy rare earths and related magnets under export licensing through Announcement No. 18. The European Central Bank (ECB) recorded that Chinese shipments of rare earth magnets fell by approximately 75% year on year in May 2025, and some carmakers paused production. In October 2025, Announcement No. 61 reached abroad, requiring foreign exporters to obtain a Chinese license for goods containing 0.1% or more by value of controlled Chinese-origin rare earth material.
Much then depends on reading these instruments precisely, since a licensing requirement is a gate that can be opened, slowed or shut. As of October 26, 2026, No. 18 remains in force. Announcement No. 70 suspended No. 61 and five related notices until November 10, 2026, and Announcement No. 72 suspended the US-specific gallium, germanium and antimony clause of No. 46 until November 27, 2026, leaving its military end-use ban intact. Beijing has since opened a reporting system for violations of strategic-mineral export rules, including transshipment through third countries. In September 2026, the two governments agreed to extend the Kuala Lumpur arrangement to January 10, 2027, but MOFCOM's announcement index shows no notice yet amending the November 10 date.
The legal record establishes capacity; motive is a separate question, and here Beijing's stated rationale and outside readings diverge. No. 18 cites the need "为维护国家安全和利益、履行防扩散等国际义务," which translates as safeguarding national security and interests and fulfilling international obligations such as non-proliferation. ECB economists judged the April measures to have been "introduced in retaliation for increased US tariffs on Chinese goods" and concluded that China "has shown its willingness to use these elements to pressure trading partners." The IEA recalls that China's 2010 quotas and licensing sent rare earth prices temporarily up by as much as ten times before they were ruled non-compliant with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. Both readings can hold at once, since non-proliferation concerns are real for dual-use materials. The record does not show a permanent embargo; licensing, suspension and negotiated extension have been used as dials.
Export restrictions are often described as a Chinese instrument, yet several countries that mine what China refines use their own versions to capture more of the value chain. Indonesia stopped exports of nickel ore below 1.7% nickel content from January 1, 2020. The DRC's strategic minerals regulator replaced a cobalt export suspension with quotas from October 16, 2025, set at 7,250 metric tons for each of November and December and reviewable according to each firm's contribution to local value chains; the IEA attributes much of a roughly 130% rise in cobalt prices to those restrictions. Zimbabwe, which halted lithium concentrate shipments in February 2026, has reaffirmed a full ban from January 2027. The European Union (EU) has signaled restrictions on exports of permanent-magnet scrap, still at the proposal stage. Argentina shows the opposite model, open exports plus investment incentives, approving lithium expansions such as a 9,500-metric-ton-a-year addition at the Fenix project under its Large Investment Incentive Regime (RIGI).
Where producer countries restrict exports to capture more value from their resources, consumer economies have relied more heavily on trade measures to reduce their exposure to concentrated supply. The US record illustrates both the reach and the limits of that response. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) raised Section 301 tariffs on Chinese natural graphite and permanent magnets to 25% from 2026. In January 2026, Proclamation 11001 under Section 232 imposed no new tariff. It directed negotiations, told officials to "consider price floors for trade in critical minerals and other trade-restricting measures," and stated the diagnosis plainly: "Mining a mineral domestically does not safeguard the national security of the United States if the United States remains dependent on a foreign country for the processing of that mineral." A plurilateral agreement built on border-adjusted price floors remains a proposal without a released text.
Washington's own diagnosis points to processing, which raises the question of whether capital to build it is arriving at the pace the tariffs assume. Critical mineral investment declined by 9% in 2025, and battery-metal capital spending fell by more than 20%. Public finance commitments in advanced economies reached around US$65 billion, yet the IEA sees "a considerable gap" between commitments and disbursements. The pipelines are lopsided too: diversified rare earth refining capacity equals around two-thirds of expected mined supply by 2035, planned magnet output only one-third. A tariff reprices an imported magnet on day one; a plant still on the drawing board cannot answer that signal.
When tariffs arrive before capacity, users bear the cost, and how heavily depends on the minerals' share of final prices, where the IEA narrows the inflation worry. Critical minerals account for around one-quarter of battery cell costs but only about 3% of the price of an average EV. Tripling rare earth prices would add about 0.1% to the cost of a car; tripling battery material prices would lift EV and storage prices by around 5%. Tariffs on such inputs tend to produce a one-time shift in the price level, and USTR's four-year review cited analyses finding minimal impacts on economy-wide prices and employment. ECB research also found that pass-through from intermediate to consumer goods prices usually takes more than one year and can be partly absorbed in margins. Sustained inflation would require restrictions

articles.title: Copper Miner Sandfire Resources (ASX:SFR) Ends Dividend Drought - Kalkine Media
articles.summary: Copper Miner Sandfire Resources (ASX:SFR) Ends Dividend Drought  Kalkine Media
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Sandfire Resources delivered a strong September quarter, with healthy sales revenue, robust underlying earnings and a comfortable net cash position.
- The copper producer paid its first fully franked dividend in several years, funded largely from the quarters free cash flow.
- Full-year production, cost and capital expenditure guidance was retained, with exploration, solar construction and study work all progressing.
Copper has quietly become one of the most closely watched commodities on the australian stock market, and this week one of its best-known producers gave the market plenty to talk about. Sandfire Resources Limited (ASX:SFR) Basic Materials Sandfire Resources Ltd (ASX:SFR) 19.64 AUD +0.455 2.372% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T04:10:00Z , a diversified copper miner and ASX 100 constituent with operations in Spain and Botswana, released its September quarter update. It showed solid sales, strong margins and a return to shareholder payouts after a long pause. For a company that spent recent years building and bedding down major assets, the update reads like a turning point. The question many are now asking is what comes next.
A Quarter Built on Consistency
Sandfires latest report is not a story of one dramatic breakthrough. It reflects steady, disciplined execution across both of its core operations, the MATSA copper complex in southern Spain and the Motheo copper mine in Botswanas Kalahari Copper Belt.
The company reported strong group copper equivalent production for the September quarter, putting it firmly on track against its full-year guidance range. MATSA contributed the larger share of output, while Motheo continued to show it can operate as a dependable second engine for the group.
What stands out is the tone of predictability. Sandfire has framed its operational approach around getting the basics right, and the quarter suggests that focus is paying off. Mining companies are often judged on surprises, both good and bad. Sandfires update was notable for having very few unwelcome ones.
MATSA Keeps the Engine Running
MATSA remains the heart of Sandfires portfolio. The Spanish operation, which processes ore from several underground mines in the Iberian Pyrite Belt, delivered the bulk of the groups copper equivalent output during the quarter.
Underlying operating costs per tonne at MATSA remained within expectations, supporting the strong margin profile reported at group level. For a polymetallic operation producing copper, zinc and lead, keeping costs contained while volumes stay steady is a meaningful achievement.
Motheo Proves Its Worth
Motheo, located in Botswana, has been one of Sandfires most important growth projects of recent years. The operations contribution to group production during the quarter underlines how far it has come since construction.
Motheos unit operating costs were notably lower than MATSAs, reflecting the different nature of the open-pit operation. Together, the two assets give Sandfire geographic diversity and a balanced production base across Europe and southern Africa.
Strong Prices Meet Lean Treatment Charges
One of the key drivers behind Sandfires healthy quarter was the broader market backdrop. Copper prices have been buoyant, supported by steady demand linked to electrification, renewable energy infrastructure and grid upgrades worldwide.
Sandfire also benefited from record low treatment and refining charges, often called TCRCs. These are the fees miners pay smelters to process copper concentrate into refined metal. When smelter capacity is tight and concentrate supply is constrained, those charges fall. That means miners keep a larger share of the value of each tonne they ship.
The combination of firm prices and lean processing fees helped Sandfire generate solid group sales revenue and strong underlying EBITDA for the quarter. The company reported an underlying EBITDA margin well above half of revenue, a figure that places it among the more profitable operators in the ASX Metal & Mining Stocks space this reporting period.
The Dividend Makes a Comeback
For shareholders, the headline moment of the quarter was the dividend. Sandfire paid a fully franked dividend during the period, its first in several years.
That return to payouts matters for a few reasons. It signals confidence in the balance sheet, reflects the cash-generating ability of the two operating mines, and marks a shift from a heavy build phase into a phase where returns can flow back to owners.
Importantly, the company noted that the dividend was effectively funded out of quarterly free cash flow. Sandfire finished the period in a net cash position only modestly below where it stood at the end of June. In other words, the payout did not meaningfully dent the companys financial flexibility.
For those who follow ASX dividend stocks, Sandfires re-entry into the dividend club is a development worth noting. Mining dividends can be cyclical and depend heavily on commodity prices, so the sustainability of future payouts will depend on how markets and operations evolve.
A Healthy Balance Sheet Behind the Payout
Sandfires net cash position at the end of September remained comfortable. That figure is significant given the companys history. Not long ago, Sandfire was carrying debt associated with the acquisition of MATSA and the construction of Motheo.
Moving into a net cash position gives the miner more room to fund exploration, advance studies and absorb any short-term volatility in copper prices without leaning on external funding.
Guidance Holds Firm
Sandfire retained its full-year guidance across production, costs and capital expenditure. That may sound unremarkable, but in the mining sector, reaffirming guidance after the first quarter is a quietly reassuring signal.
It suggests both operations are performing as planned and that managements earlier assumptions remain intact. For a sector where weather, equipment, labour and geology can all disrupt plans, steadiness has real value.
The company indicated it remains on track to meet its production and cost targets for the financial year. A further update is expected alongside its half-year results.
Exploration Moves Up a Gear
While the operating mines produce the cash, exploration shapes the future. Sandfire continued investing in both regional exploration and near-mine drilling during the quarter.
La Juliana Grabs Attention
Near-mine and extension drilling delivered encouraging results at La Juliana, a deposit located near the MATSA operations. Discoveries close to existing infrastructure are particularly valuable for miners, as they can often be developed more efficiently by using existing processing plants, roads and power.
Sandfire said it plans to accelerate drilling at La Juliana in the months ahead.
A4 Underground in Focus
In Botswana, the company also flagged plans to accelerate drilling at the A4 Underground target at Motheo. Expanding below the current open-pit operations could extend mine life and support the long-term production profile of the Botswana asset.
Kalkaroo Study Timeline
Closer to home, Sandfire continues to work on the Kalkaroo Copper-Gold Project in South Australia. The company aims to complete a pre-feasibility study in the second half of the following financial year, although recent weather-related delays have affected progress. Kalkaroo represents a longer-dated growth option that could add an Australian production base to the portfolio over time.
Solar Power and the Decarbonisation Push
Sustainability is becoming a central part of mining strategy, and Sandfire is no exception. Construction of dedicated solar facilities at both MATSA and Motheo remains on schedule.
These facilities are designed to support the companys decarbonisation goals while improving energy security at each site. Mining is energy intensive, and reducing reliance on grid electricity or diesel can help lower both emissions and operating costs over time.
Sandfire expects to commission the new solar facilities in the second half of the financial year. Once operational, they should support the companys long-term cost profile and environmental credentials, both of which are increasingly scrutinised by global customers and capital markets.
Black Butte Under Review
Sandfire also confirmed ongoing financial support for Sandfire America, which owns the Black Butte Copper Project in Montana in the United States. The project is currently reviewing its strategic options.
Black Butte has been a long-running development project for Sandfire. The outcome of the strategic review will be worth watching, as it could shape how the company allocates capital between its existing operations, exploration and development assets.
How the Shares Have Travelled
Sandfire shares have performed strongly over the past year, outpacing the broader benchmark, which has softened over the same period. The miners operational consistency, improving balance sheet and leverage to copper prices have all contributed to that relative strength.
Of course, past share price movements are not a guide to future performance. Copper markets can shift quickly in response to global economic conditions, Chinese demand, supply disruptions and interest rate settings.
The Bigger Picture for Copper Miners
Sandfires quarter arrives at a time when copper is attracting renewed attention across global markets. The metal is essential to electric vehicles, wind and solar installations, data centres and electricity networks. At the same time, new copper supply has been slow to come online, with declining ore grades and long development timelines constraining output across the industry.
That backdrop has supported prices and given established producers like Sandfire a favourable environment to operate in. Low treatment charges, while beneficial to miners, also reflect tightness in the concentrate market, a reminder of how stretched global copper supply chains have become.

articles.title: KPM Lights Up Africa's Largest Green Mining Power Grid on the DRC's Power-Short Copper Belt - Shanghai Metals Market
articles.summary: KPM Lights Up Africa's Largest Green Mining Power Grid on the DRC's Power-Short Copper Belt  Shanghai Metals Market
articles.full_text:
Likasi, DRC — October 7
On the southern edge of the DRC's copper belt, there is a question every operator learns to live with: not how much ore is in the ground, but how much electricity will arrive today. Kaipeng Mining (KPM) has answered it in an unusual way — by building a grid of its own.
On October 7, the company commissioned Phase II of its new energy power system. Comprising 440 MWp of solar capacity and 300 MW/900 MWh of grid-forming energy storage, and tied together by more than ten interconnection lines into a ring-configured internal grid, it is the mine’s dedicated renewable power system currently in operation anywhere in Africa's mining regions. The idea is as simple as it sounds: if any one line fails, the power simply flows around it.
Technically, Phase II pioneered the "unit–station–cluster" coordinated control strategy, completed full-scenario real-time digital simulator (RTDS) validation, and passed unplanned off-grid tests under all operating conditions, ultimately achieving seamless switching between grid-connected and islanded modes together with prolonged stable islanded operation. When operating at full load, the renewable power it generates can meet the power demand for its metallurgical operations, with annual clean power supply of up to 750 GWh, KPM says. That is roughly 240,000 tonnes of standard coal equivalent saved each year.
Why a mine would build a power company
None of this exists for its own sake. Mining along the Katanga copper-cobalt belt has long run up against a triple constraint, with each component raising costs for the next.
The first is the public grid. The DRC's power supply is heavily dependent on hydropower, while installed capacity and transmission capability have lagged far behind the needs of its mining regions. According to public disclosure by Ivanhoe Mines, Kamoa-Kakula — among the region's best-positioned copper mines — assessed measures including cross-border transmission upgrades from Zambia and battery storage after grid stability disturbances affected its operations from late 2022. For most mines here, an unstable grid is not an emergency. It is a line item in every production plan.
The second is the weather. The country's hydro resources are concentrated at the Inga Falls complex, more than 1,000 kilometres from the mining belt. Ageing generators at Inga I and II, deferred maintenance and the long-stalled Inga III expansion have kept actual output well below nameplate capacity; when the dry season arrives, a power shortfall follows.
The third is geography. The DRC is landlocked: its mining belt hauls diesel and sulphur thousands of kilometres overland from distant seaports such as Dar es Salaam and Durban. Sulphuric acid is an even tighter bottleneck: every tonne of cathode copper produced through SX-EW process requires 3.5 to 4.5 tonnes of acid, and around 90% of the region's imported sulphur moves through Middle East shipping routes. In the first half of 2026, amid geopolitical tensions and changes in export policy, acid prices in the mining region spiked to $1,000–1,400 per tonne at one point, and chemical delivery times stretched from about three months to between four and six months, forcing a number of producers to cut output when input supplies ran short.
Today, the competitive logic of DRC mining has been completely rewritten: the contest is no longer only about mineral rights and ore grades, but about who holds a stable supply of power and acid — and who, as a result, holds the better position on the cost curve.
From backup power to the main source
KPM's mine-dedicated green microgrid was not built alone. KPM leads investment and operations while Chinese power-control specialist NR Electric is responsible for technical planning and the supply of core grid-forming energy storage and dispatch equipment.
Phase I — described by KPM as the first large-scale renewable power system built for mine operating conditions in the DRC — achieved full-capacity grid connection on schedule and met its reliability targets, despite constrained cross-border logistics and underdeveloped local infrastructure. Phase II followed within the same year, and the upgrade changed the system's role rather than merely its size: voltage levels were raised, the solar-storage-diesel ratio re-optimised, and grid-forming storage expanded to 300 MW/900 MWh. A supplementary source became the mine's primary one — no longer a helper to the weak public grid, but the load-bearing source underneath the entire mining and metallurgical operations.
The hard part is invisible. Coordinating wide-area, multi-node grid-forming storage clusters is a recognised control problem across the industry. For Phase II, the project team applied a hierarchical "unit–station–cluster" control strategy, which the developer says reduces the coupling between node count and control complexity from exponential to linear. Before commissioning, the system passed full-scenario real-time digital simulator (RTDS) validation and unplanned off-grid tests under all operating conditions.
KPM adds that its solution has since been used as a technical reference in the renewable-integration plans of more than 30 miners.
The loop that closes on site
The power system is one leg of a larger design. This year, KPM brought three flagship projects on stream: the solar-storage system, an oxidative roasting-leaching line that recovers value from refractory mixed copper and cobalt ores while producing sulphuric acid as a by-product, and a dedicated sulphur-burning acid plant that secures on-site acid supply for hydrometallurgy. Each one covers a constraint the others expose — power for high-load roasting and electrowinning, acid for leaching, processing capacity for the mine's complex ores.
The economics, ultimately, are what carry the case. The solar-storage architecture covers round-the-clock demand; the closed loop of power, roasting, acid and hydrometallurgy keeps production stable when external markets are not. As the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is phased in, KPM notes, green-powered metallurgy puts the operation in a stronger position to manage the associated cost — one that competitors are only just starting to price in.
Competition in global mining has long since shifted from "who secured the ore" to "who can turn ore into product at lower overall cost and with a more stable supply chain." Under the Congolese sun, 440 MW of solar panels now tilt toward the answer. The diesel units still stand at the edge of the plant, silent until called. For one mine on the copper belt, the question of "how much electricity will arrive today" has, at last, a different answer: as much as it needs.

Background on DRC power, sulphur and sulphuric acid markets draws on public reporting by Caixin, Reuters and industry research firms.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia is building its gas business at home and its LNG business abroad - EnterpriseAM
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia is building its gas business at home and its LNG business abroad  EnterpriseAM
articles.full_text:
Is Saudi Arabia building its biggest new gas field to export? Not for now, analysts tell EnterpriseAM: Saudi power plants and industry can absorb most of the new gas. The gas also lets Saudi Arabia sell crude it now burns for power. to be sold abroad: at peak, the program is expected to displace about 500k bbl/d of crude, Aramco has said, Reuters reported.
Gas exports are a later question, and the likelier exit is the Red Sea, outside Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has no LNG export terminal or cross-border gas export pipeline today. A modular terminal at Yanbu could be delivered within three to five years of an investment decision, Kate Dourian, a board member at the Energy Institute’s Middle East branch, tells us.
Jafurah is the supply end of that chain: Aramco began production in December 2025 and is targeting 2 bn cf/d of sales gas by 2030, alongside substantial volumes of ethane and gas liquids, as part of an expansion that could raise its sales gas production capacity by around 80% from 2021 levels. It expects the expansion to add USD 12-15 bn in annual cashflow by 2030.
Domestic demand first
Domestic demand is expected to absorb much of the additional gas: The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects Saudi Arabia’s gas output to expand by almost 40 bcm between 2024 and 2030, while gas-to-power demand is forecast to grow by more than 40% by 2030, according to a 2025 IEA analysis (pdf). The additional gas is expected to support the shift away from oil-fired power generation and feed industrial expansion, and new AI and data center developments will add to electricity demand.
Analysts disagree on how much gas will be left over: Wood Mackenzie estimates Saudi Arabia could eventually have as much as 50 bcm of spare gas a year if production reaches 180 bcm. “This is unlikely to generate a substantial surplus given how much gas is required to displace oil from the power generation sector, and the scale of industrial growth in the Kingdom. Saudi Arabia has a huge demand capacity to absorb extra gas volumes,” Jamie Ingram, managing editor at Middle East Economic Survey (MEES), tells us.
Jafurah alone wouldn’t replace the oil still burned for power: Saudi power plants generated roughly 300 TWh from natural gas in 2025, against about 150 TWh from oil and 20 TWh from renewables, Anne-Sophie Corbeau, global research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, tells us. Even without additional industrial and data center demand, Jafurah’s planned production wouldn’t be enough to replace the remaining oil-fired generation, she says, so Saudi Arabia would need other gas developments alongside renewables to complete the transition.
Crude freed for export
Saudi Arabia is already working to stop burning its exports: Its Liquid Fuel Displacement Program aims to replace more than 1 mn bbl/d of liquid fuels across electricity generation, desalination, manufacturing, and agriculture by 2030, with investment going into gas-fired power plants, fuel conversions, and renewables. Aramco’s expanding gas network is meant to supply customers that used to rely on oil, and every barrel of crude displaced from domestic consumption is potentially available for export.
Power generation is the best first use of the new gas: Combined-cycle gas plants can run at up to 60% efficiency, against about 30% for crude-fired plants, Rystad Energy says, and they supply cheaper electricity to the industries Riyadh is trying to develop. That makes domestic power the most economically attractive immediate use of additional gas, ahead of new LNG export infrastructure, Ingram argues.
Aramco can now produce gas without producing crude, which helped during the conflict. Saudi Arabia historically relied heavily on associated gas produced alongside crude oil, Dourian says. “The development of non-associated gas fields such as Jafurah gives Aramco greater flexibility because gas output is no longer so closely tied to crude production.” That mattered when Saudi Arabia curtailed oil production during the regional conflict. “Non-associated gas production has helped limit the impact on domestic gas supplies,” Dourian adds.
From field to factory
Aramco is spending USD 8.8 bn to move the gas. Phase III of its Master Gas System adds 3.1 bn cf/d of transmission capacity by 2028 through roughly 4k km of pipelines and 17 gas compression trains, meant to carry additional supply to power plants and industrial customers across the Kingdom as Jafurah and other gas developments ramp up.
Contractors are building Jafurah in phases: A Hyundai Engineering-Hyundai E&C consortium has completed the first phase of its gas-processing facilities under a USD 1.6 bn contract and is working on phase two under a USD 2.3 bn award. EPC work for phase four has begun, and contractors have submitted bids for phase five. The Fadhili Gas Plant expansion, another major part of Aramco’s gas program, is scheduled for completion in 2027.
Pipelines and customers have to grow together, Dourian says. Phase III covers much of the transmission capacity the current plan requires, and growth after 2030 could need a fourth expansion alongside additional processing and liquids-handling facilities. The harder part is coordinating upstream development, transmission capacity, and new industrial customers so that gas reaches demand centers as it becomes available. “I would expect midstream capacity and the timing of downstream projects to become increasingly important considerations as production expands, rather than assuming that the availability of gas reserves will be the main constraint,” Dourian says.
Who owns the midstream
Aramco has sold investors a stake in Jafurah’s gas processing and kept control. It closed a USD 11 bn lease-and-leaseback last year. Jafurah Midstream Gas Company holds the development and operating rights to the Jafurah gas plant and the Riyas NGL fractionation facility and leases them back to Aramco for 20 years, with a BlackRock GIP-led consortium holding 49% and Aramco holding 51% and operational control. Aramco also plans to turn its gas business into a standalone division and is weighing a minority listing. The division would cover domestic operations and international LNG, and Bloomberg reported that Evercore is advising on a structure that could value the business above USD 100 bn.
The neighbors’ head start
Aramco is building an LNG business with other countries’ gas before it has substantial domestic volumes to export. It has invested USD 500 mn in MidOcean Energy, signed long-term offtake agreements covering US LNG projects — including 1 mtpa from Commonwealth LNG in Louisiana, with an option to double that volume — and outlined an ambition to market 20 mtpa of LNG globally, with 4.5 mtpa in progress as of January. That experience could eventually support a Saudi export business if domestic production creates a surplus, Ingram says.
Adnoc and QatarEnergy already have the infrastructure and customers Saudi Arabia would need to compete with. Adnoc’s 9.6 mtpa Ruwais LNG project has committed more than 90% of planned capacity under long-term arrangements, with its first trains expected online in 2H 2028. QatarEnergy is targeting 142 mtpa of LNG capacity by 2030 through its North Field expansion, although regional conflict has damaged existing facilities and disrupted the expansion schedule. Saudi Arabia could build an export business, but it would enter a market where neighboring producers already have a head start in liquefaction, customers, and long-term contracts.
Saudi industry can compete with those neighbors before Saudi Arabia exports a cargo. Jafurah is expected to produce 420 mn cf/d of ethane and around 630k b/d of natural gas liquids and condensate by 2030, adding feedstock for petrochemicals and other industries alongside the additional sales gas. Saudi manufacturers get more access to energy and feedstock while Aramco frees up crude for export, which could strengthen their position against UAE and Qatari industries long before the first Saudi LNG cargo.
An exit outside Hormuz
Saudi Arabia would never match Qatar’s scale, but it could offer a route outside Hormuz, Ingram says. “Saudi Arabia would never be an exporter on the scale of Qatar, but what Saudi Arabia could potentially provide would be export capability outside the Strait of Hormuz on the Red Sea,” he says. Rather than matching Qatar’s liquefaction capacity, Saudi Arabia could compete by providing an alternative supply route to European buyers, he adds.
The modular terminal would give Saudi Arabia access to global markets without committing immediately to a large conventional LNG complex, Dourian says. Regional pipelines could require less capital, depending on their routes, but would offer less flexibility in reaching different customers, she adds.
Why this matters: Jafurah’s most immediate export payoff is the crude it frees up, which will put the gas division's international LNG ambitions ahead of its domestic export capacity, even as Aramco builds a business that could be valued above USD 100 bn.

articles.full_text:
High production costs, limited commissioned capacity and infrastructure gaps remain key barriers to scaling green hydrogen, despite India’s 5 million-tonne annual production target, according to the report by rating agency.
                                    
                    
                    
                    
                                        India’s green hydrogen sector could attract investments of $180 billion to $200 billion by 2030, but high production costs and infrastructure constraints continue to hamper large-scale deployment, according to a report by CareEdge-ESG Ratings released on Monday.
The report, "Why Green Hydrogen Is Becoming an Industrial Strategy Question", said green hydrogen is becoming increasingly important for India’s industrial competitiveness, energy security and export prospects, particularly in steel, fertilisers, refining and chemicals.
India aims to produce at least 5 million metric tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030 under the National Green Hydrogen Mission, launched in January 2023 with an outlay of ₹19,744 crore. However, only around 8,000 tonnes per year of production capacity had been commissioned by February 2026, the report said.
Production costs remain a key hurdle
Green hydrogen currently costs around ₹350-450 per kg, compared with ₹160-200 per kg for conventional grey hydrogen. The report expects costs to decline to about $2.4 per kg by 2030 as renewable electricity becomes cheaper, electrolyser costs fall and projects scale up.
Fertilisers and steel are expected to be key demand drivers. India consumes around 17-19 million metric tonnes of ammonia annually, largely produced using natural gas. Green ammonia could help reduce fossil fuel import dependence and emissions.
A Solar Energy Corporation of India auction in August 2025 discovered a benchmark price of ₹49.75 per kg for green ammonia. However, execution challenges and the withdrawal of two of the 13 offtakers highlight the difficulties in converting price discovery into operational projects.
CBAM raises pressure on steel exporters
The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is increasing the economic implications of carbon intensity for Indian exporters, the report said.
Indian steel exporters could face estimated costs of $70-190 per metric tonne on shipments to the European Union. These costs could exceed $270 per metric tonne where default emissions values apply, according to the analysis.
India produced approximately 164.9 million metric tonnes of steel in 2025, making it the world’s second-largest steel producer, based on provisional figures cited in the report.
Infrastructure and certification critical to scale-up
The report said scaling green hydrogen will require investment in storage, pipelines, port infrastructure and reliable offtake agreements. It also highlighted the need for international alignment on renewable electricity sourcing and emissions verification to support exports.
India introduced its Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme in 2025 to provide a framework for traceability. Dependence on imported electrolyser components, including membranes, catalysts and stacks, also highlights the need to develop domestic manufacturing capabilities.
Corporate investment commitments indicate growing interest in the sector. Reliance Industries has announced ₹75,000 crore for an integrated green energy ecosystem, while Adani Enterprises has stated an investment commitment exceeding $50 billion over the next decade for green hydrogen. NTPC has also proposed a green hydrogen hub in Andhra Pradesh.
However, the report said actual deployment would depend on financial closure, commercially viable operating models and assured demand.
Globally, announced low-emissions hydrogen projects could deliver 27 million tonnes per annum by 2030. Operational projects, those under construction and those at final investment decision or with a strong likelihood of commissioning account for slightly more than 6 million tonnes per annum, the report said.
Nikunj Dube, chief ratings officer at CareEdge-ESG, said commercially viable projects, competitive production costs, reliable offtake agreements and robust infrastructure would determine the pace of adoption.

articles.summary: What are the sources of LNG supply for Vietnam's electricity production?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Vietnam has several options for importing liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Middle East, Asia-Pacific, and Russia. However, each source of supply has its own advantages and risks.
The revised Power Development Plan VIII anticipates the development of 15 LNG power projects with a total capacity of over 25.6 GW. Therefore, ensuring a stable and long-term supply of LNG at competitive prices is a critical requirement for the efficient operation of these projects, contributing to national energy security.
Global LNG supply continues to expand.
According to a report by the Ministry of Industry and Trade assessing the potential for LNG imports for electricity production, global natural gas reserves are expected to reach approximately 209 trillion cubic meters by the end of 2024. Of this, Russia has the largest reserves with nearly 47 trillion cubic meters, followed by Iran with nearly 34 trillion cubic meters, Qatar with 23.8 trillion cubic meters, and the United States with nearly 18 trillion cubic meters.
The United States has been the world's largest producer of natural gas for many years, with production reaching 925-1,073 billion cubic meters per year between 2020 and 2025. Russia ranks second, maintaining production of 586-702 billion cubic meters per year. Other major gas producers include Canada, Norway , Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and China.
Alongside exploration activities, global LNG production capacity continues to expand. By the end of 2025, total liquefaction capacity is expected to reach 524.5 million tonnes per year, an increase of 30.1 million tonnes compared to 2024. The United States, Australia, and Qatar are among the world's leading liquefaction capacity providers.
In 2025 alone, the United States exported 110.74 million tons of LNG, accounting for approximately 25% of total global LNG production. This was followed by Qatar with 81.5 million tons, Australia with 80.3 million tons, Russia with 30.5 million tons, and Malaysia with 28.8 million tons.
Conversely, around 50 countries are expected to import LNG in 2025, primarily concentrated in Asia and Europe. China continues to be the largest import market with 69.77 million tons, although this is down 8.9 million tons from the previous year. Other major markets include Japan , Taiwan, and France.
Currently, Vietnam has the Thi Vai LNG terminal with a receiving capacity of 1 million tons/year, expected to be increased to 3 million tons/year, and the Cai Mep LNG port with a capacity of approximately 3 million tons/year.
Besides infrastructure investment, long-term LNG supply contracts have also been signed, including a contract with Shell to supply approximately 400,000 tons of LNG per year from 2027 to 2031.
The Middle East has significant potential to supply LNG.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Middle East, especially Qatar, has the potential to become a major source of LNG for Vietnam thanks to its abundant reserves, large production capacity, and well-developed export infrastructure.
In 2025, LNG from Qatar will account for approximately 26.4% of Vietnam's total LNG imports.
Qatar's LNG production is concentrated in the industrial city of Ras Laffan, which has a large-scale LNG liquefaction and export infrastructure, combined with CO2 capture and storage facilities.
You may also like
Qatar is developing the North Field East and North Field South projects, which are expected to increase total liquefaction capacity to approximately 142 million tonnes per year by 2030.
In terms of transportation, the distance from Qatar to Vietnam is greater than from Indonesia, Malaysia, and Russia, but shorter than shipping routes from the United States.
However, LNG supplies from the Middle East also pose geopolitical risks. LNG exports from Qatar to Vietnam must pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a shipping lane sensitive to political and security instability in the region.
This necessitates a balance between economies of scale and the ability to ensure stable transportation when choosing to import LNG from the Middle East.
Australia and Malaysia have advantages in transportation.
Besides the Middle East, the Asia-Pacific region has many potential LNG suppliers for Vietnam, notably Australia, Malaysia, and Indonesia.
Australia has natural gas reserves of approximately 4 trillion cubic meters. Although significantly lower than Qatar, the country remains one of the world's largest exporters of LNG.
In 2025, Australia will export 80.3 million tonnes of LNG, ranking third globally, accounting for nearly 19% of global exports and roughly matching Qatar's production.
Major LNG projects are concentrated in Western Australia, including North West Shelf LNG with a capacity of 16.9 million tonnes/year, Gorgon LNG with 15.6 million tonnes/year, and Wheatstone LNG with 8.9 million tonnes/year.
Australia's advantage lies in its export port system located on international shipping routes, facilitating the transportation of LNG to Asian markets, including Vietnam. Importantly, these shipping routes do not pass through geopolitical bottlenecks such as the Strait of Hormuz.
However, Australia's future LNG export capacity may be impacted by domestic energy security policies, including the Australian Gas Security Mechanism (ADGSM).
For Malaysia, the biggest advantage is its geographical proximity to Vietnam.
In 2025, Malaysia exported 28.8 million tons of LNG, ranking fifth in the world. The country's LNG infrastructure is mainly concentrated in the Bintulu complex in Sarawak state.
The shipping distance from Bintulu to the Southeast region of Vietnam is only about 1,000-1,500 nautical miles, making it one of the shortest shipping routes among international LNG suppliers.
However, the long-term outlook for LNG imports from Malaysia also faces challenges. According to information cited by the Ministry of Industry and Trade from the International Energy Agency (IEA), some of Malaysia's traditional gas fields have entered a decline phase, while domestic gas demand tends to increase.
You may also like
Therefore, Malaysia's LNG exports are projected to increase slowly or decrease slightly in the long term unless more large-scale gas projects come online.
Supply from Russia is affected by sanctions.
Russia possesses the world's largest natural gas reserves, with nearly 47 trillion cubic meters, accounting for approximately 21% of total global reserves.
Russia's gas resources are mainly located in Siberia, the Yamal Peninsula, and Sakhalin Island. Average annual production is approximately 640-650 billion cubic meters.
Previously, Russian natural gas was primarily exported to Europe via pipelines. However, after 2022, as European demand for Russian gas declined sharply, Russia accelerated its shift towards exporting LNG, particularly to Asian markets.
According to its Energy Strategy to 2050, Russia aims to increase its total LNG capacity to approximately 90-100 million tons per year by 2030.
Despite the potential for large supply sources, achieving this goal is proving difficult due to sanctions from the United States and the European Union.
Thus, the Ministry of Industry and Trade's assessment shows that Vietnam has the potential to access many international LNG sources, but each market has certain limitations. Qatar has the advantage of production scale, Australia and Malaysia have favorable transportation conditions, while supply from Russia is affected by sanctions.
Diversifying import markets, developing receiving infrastructure, and signing long-term supply contracts are therefore factors that need to be considered to ensure fuel supply for electricity production.

articles.title: Camino moves towards building its first copper mine as supply tightens - Kitco
articles.summary: Camino moves towards building its first copper mine as supply tightens  Kitco
articles.full_text:
View of the Puquios copper project in Chile.
- Camino's Puquios copper project in Chile is permitted to start construction, with key water infrastructure now authorized to proceed.
- With Camino and partner Nittetsu Mining advancing talks on a potential Japanese-sourced debt facility, Camino is targeting a construction decision in Chile before the end of 2026.
- In Peru, a newly approved permit nearly doubles Camino's exploration ground at Costa de Cobre, increasing the effective exploration area by approximately 94%, from 6,012.50 hectares to 11,671.90 hectares, across three copper trends.
Disseminated on Behalf of: Camino Corp.
The copper market has no shortage of deposits, but it lacks mines ready to be built.
Demand is climbing fast as electric vehicles, power grids, and AI data centres pull on an already stretched supply chain. Global consumption is forecast to nearly double and reach 56 million tonnes a year by 2050.
Supply is struggling to keep up, with several of the world's largest producers mining lower grades and new projects taking many years longer to come online. A discovery made today could take a decade or more to produce its first tonne of copper.
Investors have noticed, and analysts at Paradigm Capital say the key question in mining has shifted from how big a deposit is to whether it can actually be permitted, financed, and built. Paradigm acted as a co-lead agent on Camino's C$5.8 million brokered financing in August 2026.
Camino Corp. (TSXV: COR | OTCQB: CAMZF) has a ready answer.
Its flagship Puquios copper project in Chile is permitted for construction and owned 50/50 with Japan's Nittetsu Mining, an established Chilean copper producer. In southern Peru, the company is exploration drilling the Costa de Cobre project with Nittetsu, which holds a 35% interest. Camino envisions the project as potentially its second copper mine, although it is still at the exploration and discovery stage. Two more Peruvian projects, Maria Cecilia and Plata Dorada, round out the pipeline.
A Japanese debt facility and an equity financing package are the final steps toward a construction decision. Once both are in place, Camino plans to make the jump from explorer to builder, a move CEO Jay Chmelauskas says few copper mining companies are in a position to make.
"There's really only a handful of copper companies with projects that are construction ready, and ready to receive capital and build," he said.
Set up for a fast start
Roadwork widening to receive heavy equipment at the Puquios mine site, Chile.
Puquios sits at a low elevation about 130 kilometres northeast of La Serena, with an unsealed highway running within two kilometres of the site.
The mining method is simple: ore is crushed, stacked on lined pads, and rinsed with a solution that dissolves the copper, which is then plated on site into high-purity copper sheets called cathode. Camino will sell finished metal, with no smelter required.
The 2025 pre-feasibility study (PFS) outlines a 14.2-year mine producing about 8,800 tonnes of copper a year through its first eight years. Copper prices have since increased above the PFS base-case assumption, with copper currently trading at approximately US$6.67/lb as at October 13, 2026, and the market outlook is supported by tightening supply and expectations for continued growth.
The mine plan draws on Proven and Probable reserves of 26 million tonnes grading 0.49% copper, estimated at a copper price of US$4.28/lb, and supports annual production of up to 9,000 tonnes of copper cathode over a 14.2-year mine life.
NI 43-101 Key Project Highlights (PFS):
- After-Tax NPV (8%): US$118 million
- After-Tax IRR: 23.4%
- Copper Price Assumption: US$4.28/lb
- Initial Capital Cost: US$141.9 million
- All-in Sustaining Cost (AISC): US$2.00/lb
- Mine Life: 14.2 years
- Mineral Reserves: 25,973 kt @ 0.494% Cu
- Recovery: 78.8%
- Annual Production: up to 9,000 tonnes a year of copper cathode
A partner that has built before
Building a first mine is where many juniors stall, but Camino is taking that step alongside a partner that has done it before. Nittetsu Mining already produces copper in Chile at its Atacama Kozan mine and is developing a second operation, Arqueros. Nittetsu helped fund the Puquios acquisition and will operate the mine. Nittetsu's first investment with Camino was an earn-in to Camino's Costa de Cobre copper asset in Peru.
Partnering with Nittetsu on a second copper asset in Chile also provides access to Japanese lenders. According to Chmelauskas, Nittetsu attracted more than US$350 million in Japanese-sourced capital for the Arqueros copper mine. Camino says it remains confident about finalizing the agreements needed to unlock similar debt for Puquios, subject to final negotiations, definitive documentation, and lender approvals.
"Nittetsu provided the cash component to the transaction to secure the Puquios asset," Chmelauskas said. "They are a strong operator with a proven track record in Chile, and through our relationship, we're able to attract potentially low-cost Japanese debt."
Preparatory work is underway on the ground. On October 5, Camino announced that Chile's water authority, the Dirección General de Aguas (DGA), authorized construction of the water diversion works needed to manage surface water around the mine and its planned processing facilities. The approval followed the joint venture's posting of a US$1.7 million bond, which will be returned in full once the work is complete and certified.
"Authorization to start construction of the surface water infrastructure is a key milestone to commence the construction phase of the Puquios mine," said Marcelo Bruna, CEO of Cuprum Resources, the Camino-Nittetsu joint venture company.
The bigger prize at Puquios
Cross-section of the Puquios copper deposit, Chile.
The first mine targets only the top layer of the deposit, where weathering has concentrated copper into minerals that leach easily. That deeper system has seen only limited drilling, and further work is required to determine its extent, continuity, and economic significance. Leaching tests for the deeper system are underway at Nittetsu's research centre near Tokyo.
The expansion case is still conceptual and not yet part of a compliant resource or mine plan, but it has already drawn outside money. Elemental Royalties paid US$8 million for a 1.25% royalty on Puquios, citing its exploration potential.
"To expand the project beyond the current mine plan, Camino plans further drilling and more metallurgical testing on the deeper sulphides over the construction period," Chmelauskas said.
Envisioning a second mine taking shape in Peru
Drilling core showing oxide copper intercepts at Costa de Cobre in Peru.
Costa de Cobre covers about 23,000 hectares on Peru's southern coast, in the same copper belt as one of the country's newest large copper mines. It is an iron oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) system, a deposit type known for large, high-value copper orebodies. This is the second joint venture with Nittetsu, whereby Camino maintains a 65% interest, and Nittetsu is a 35% participating partner.
More than 28,000 metres of drilling has returned thick zones of copper, some starting right at surface. Hole DCH-097 cut 55.5 metres at 0.93% Cu from surface, including 7.5 metres at 2.58% Cu. Deeper down, DCH-012 returned 96.5 metres grading 0.93% Cu from 175 metres, including 4.5 metres at 5.01% Cu.
Camino now has far more ground to test after Peru's Ministry of Energy and Mines approved an expanded environmental permit on September 28. The approval grows the exploration area by about 94%, increasing the effective exploration area from 6,012 hectares to 11,672 hectares across three copper trends, with drilling planned to start this fall, subject to final authorization.
"We always have two targets in mind when we drill," Chmelauskas said. "One, we're drilling a near-surface copper deposit that we believe could potentially support a medium-scale soluble copper SXEW-style mine. But two, we're drilling to identify potentially larger copper sulphide mineralization."
A valuation that has not caught up
Management believes construction and exploration are what closes that gap. "Completing a final investment decision with Nittetsu and securing competitive Japanese-sourced debt for our Chile copper business, and more exploration drilling in Peru, are the next value drivers at Camino," Chmelauskas said. "We are very focused on achieving these value driver milestones and catalysts."
Over the next 12 months, investors will be watching three things: a construction decision at Puquios, fresh drilling at Costa de Cobre, and a copper market that continues to tighten.
The copper industry needs new mines, and it needs them soon to meet growing demand. Camino has one that is permitted to start construction and advancing toward a construction decision. It also has a partner to help fund it and a management team working towards unlocking the value in a second project right behind it.
