articles.full_text:
At the London Metal Exchange (LME) Week, industry experts pushed back against the increasingly bullish copper narrative, arguing that AI data centers, India’s growth story, and green-energy demand may not deliver the copper boom many expect.
The London Stock Exchange Group Data & Analytics’ director of metals research, Bruce Alway, said a calculation error appears to have overstated data center copper needs, while technologies such as fiber optics reduce copper intensity inside facilities. Similarly, India may be “the next China” in scale but not in copper intensity, because modern infrastructure is less metal-heavy and circularity is higher.
In China, construction and home-appliance demand are weakening. Although electronics, AI, and battery manufacturing hit a record Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) of 59.7 in August, China’s copper consumption growth is expected to slow to 1%–1.5% toward 2030.
Meanwhile, record-high prices above $14,000/megatonnes (mt) are not simply evidence of robust demand; they are squeezing buyers, delaying price-sensitive grid projects, and accelerating substitution. Aurubis’ Tanja Winter said customers stopped fulfilling orders after the price spike, while long 60–120-day payment cycles strain working capital.
Aluminum substitution is intensifying at a copper-to-aluminum ratio of 4.8:1, especially in air conditioning. However, Winter cautioned that panic-driven switching can be technically and functionally poor for high-precision components.
The “perfect storm” of supply disruptions from May 2025 to August 2026 is easing, but copper concentrate markets remain tight, with smelters reportedly paying miners $1,500 per tonne of refined copper. China’s overseas mining stakes and strong relationships with Chile and Peru give it an advantage. At the same time in Europe, Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) demand higher recycled content but often export their own factory scrap to China.
Overall, copper’s demand growth may still be positive, but if China slows, buyers defer purchases, and aluminum substitutions accelerate, high prices could partly destroy that demand.
Mexico’s clean-energy push trails Latin America as natural gas fills the gap
Mexico plans to nearly double its state-owned utilities’ solar and wind capacity to about 7.1GW by 2030, but clean generation is projected to rise only 9%, while gas-fired output surges 72%.
Fiscal constraints and reliance on $16.7 billion in mixed public-private contracts are slowing deployment, leaving Mexico’s 36% clean-power target well behind Brazil, Colombia, and Chile.
The plan signals meaningful renewable expansion, yet without faster delivery and a clearer gas-transition pathway, Mexico risks locking in fossil-fuel dependence just as regional competitors position themselves for green investment.
Europe faces tight window to supply MENA’s winter wheat needs
Middle East and North African buyers may need 5.56–7.06 million tonnes of wheat for November–December loading, but EU, Russian and Ukrainian export capacity looks tight, with disrupted Black Sea logistics, seasonal slowdowns and weather risks limiting supply.
Egypt’s potential purchases of up to 3.5 million tonnes are the key swing factor, while southern-hemisphere new crop is unlikely to arrive in bulk before late December.
This suggests a market vulnerable to price and freight volatility, as even a modest extra demand or a shipping disruption could quickly tighten availability and lift costs for import-dependent MENA states.
Indonesia cuts pipeline gas exports to Singapore by 9%
Indonesia has cut pipeline gas exports to Singapore by 31 Million Standard Cubic Feet per Day (MMSCFD), diverting gas from Natuna and Sumatra to power Batam, Bintan and Sumatra after recent blackouts.
Singapore says the 18-day reduction is under 2% of its daily gas demand and can import more LNG if needed, though importers may pursue contractual remedies.
The move underscores Indonesia’s growing emphasis on domestic energy security, while highlighting Singapore’s acute reliance on imported gas for electricity.

SunSirs: Super El Niño Impacts Copper Market
October 26 2026 16:34:28
A "super" El Niño event is intensifying globally. In a bulletin released on October 8, 2026, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) noted that, driven by El Niño, temperatures across much of the globe are likely to exceed historical averages. Precipitation patterns are expected to shift, increasing the risk of droughts and floods in various regions.
The ripple effects of this extreme weather have already reached the copper supply chain. Several overseas copper miners have announced production cuts or lowered their output guidance, while domestic (Chinese) listed companies are proactively developing contingency plans to hedge against climate-related risks. According to institutional analysis, El Niño affects copper supply primarily through three channels: mining operations, power supply, and land or port logistics. While it may not fundamentally reverse market trends, it acts as an "amplifier" for supply-demand imbalances in the short term.
Super El Niño Takes Shape
Extreme Climate Impacts May Persist Through 2027
Monitoring by China’s National Climate Center indicates that a super El Niño event officially formed in September. The WMO reported on October 8 that sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are set to reach record highs between October and December—a sign that the phenomenon is strengthening and will peak in December.
The WMO forecasts a near 100% probability that this El Niño event will persist until February 2027, potentially ranking as one of the strongest such events since at least 1950.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterized by rising sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. Typically occurring every two to seven years and lasting approximately 9 to 12 months, its impact on global temperatures is often most pronounced in the year following its formation. The most recent El Niño event occurred between 2023 and 2024, contributing to the record-breaking global temperatures observed in 2024. A 2026 report from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) identifies Chile, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Peru as the world’s top three copper-producing nations, with South America and Africa serving as the primary regions for copper extraction.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has indicated that with the El Niño phenomenon expected to peak in late 2026, much of the Southern Hemisphere—including Southern Africa and South America—will experience its hottest season during the first few months of 2027. The combination of seasonal heat and El Niño may heighten risks such as droughts, wildfires, and haze. Meanwhile, East African nations, including Tanzania and the Seychelles, face a significantly increased risk of flooding.
Two Major Chilean Mining Companies Announce Production Cuts
Chinese Mining Firms Build Defenses Against Drought
Following extreme weather in Chile, multinational copper producers Antofagasta and Lundin Mining have disclosed the impact of these conditions on their operations, leading to downward revisions in annual production guidance and an increase in cash costs. Similarly, Chinese A-share listed mining companies have responded to investor inquiries, outlining measures to address climate volatility, such as optimizing water-saving processes and implementing multi-energy complementary systems.
As a major global copper producer, Chile has been affected by El Niño, prompting companies with local copper assets—such as Antofagasta and Lundin Mining—to issue statements.
On July 24, Antofagasta reported that extreme weather in Chile necessitated an orderly suspension of operations at its Los Pelambres mine; production had resumed by the time the company’s semi-annual report was released. During the crisis, the Chilean government declared a "state of disaster" for the Coquimbo Region. The semi-annual report, released in August, confirmed that the mine’s restart has proceeded safely. While core equipment and infrastructure sustained no major damage, some pipeline supports and water management systems required repairs. Consequently, the group has adjusted its full-year 2026 copper production forecast to a range of 625,000–655,000 tonnes.
On August 19, Lundin Mining issued a follow-up announcement. At the Caserones mine in Chile’s Atacama region—an asset within the company’s portfolio—a second winter storm struck on August 13, following an initial round of power outages that occurred between July 18 and 30. The storm brought heavy rainfall to lower altitudes and exceptionally intense snowfall accompanied by high winds to higher elevations, resulting in further damage to a power transmission tower that had already been compromised during the previous storm. Jack Lundin, the company’s President and CEO, acknowledged that this second severe storm "interrupted recovery and repair efforts," delayed the plan for a full resumption of operations, and led to additional unplanned downtime.
Consequently, the 2026 copper production guidance for the Caserones mine has been revised downward from 130,000–140,000 tonnes to 120,000–130,000 tonnes, while the cash cost for copper has been adjusted upward from $2.05–$2.25 per pound to $2.15–$2.35 per pound. The company’s consolidated copper production guidance has been updated to 300,000–325,000 tonnes, with cash costs projected at $1.95–$2.15 per pound. Production guidance for the Candelaria mine remains unchanged.
In contrast to the direct damage experienced by operations in Chile, Chinese mining companies are primarily taking proactive measures to prepare for potential droughts triggered by the El Niño phenomenon.
On September 10, Sinomine Resource Group stated on an interactive investor platform that it is closely monitoring the impact of El Niño on water resources in Zimbabwe. At its Bikita mine, the company has enhanced water-use resilience—thereby mitigating the impact of climate fluctuations on production—by implementing measures such as recycling process water and optimizing water-saving technologies. Furthermore, in 2024, the mine completed the construction of Zimbabwe’s first multi-energy complementary system, integrating solar photovoltaic (PV) power, energy storage, grid electricity, and diesel-powered generation. This system provides a high degree of energy independence and stability, ensuring the continuity of mining operations. On September 11, Tongling Nonferrous Metals Group stated that the Mirador copper mine is actively implementing measures to ensure the continuity of its production and operations.
On September 30, GEM Co., Ltd. noted on an interactive investor platform that the company places great importance on the potential impact of the El Niño phenomenon and drought conditions on its production. It has established robust mechanisms for water supply security and responses to extreme weather. The company’s nickel resource project in Indonesia continues to operate stably. GEM will remain vigilant regarding climate change and water supply conditions at its industrial parks to ensure the stable and sustainable operation of its projects.
El Niño Acts as an Amplifier for Copper Supply-Demand Imbalances
Several institutions have recently pointed out that El Niño—which causes divergent weather patterns, including both droughts and floods—is disrupting global copper supply across three key areas: mining operations, power supply, and transportation. This has emerged as a short-term source of volatility for copper prices.
China Merchants Futures noted that key mining regions in Chile and Peru are facing heavy rainfall and mudslides, which have hindered open-pit mining and the transport of copper concentrate. Meanwhile, high temperatures have driven up demand for copper used in power grids. This climate-related shock manifests through a dual impact: flooding in some areas and drought in others. Galaxy Securities further explained that heavy rains in South American mining regions have led to temporary mine closures and damaged infrastructure. In Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where hydropower accounts for a significant share of the energy mix, droughts have resulted in tighter electricity rationing. Additionally, low water levels in the Panama Canal have driven up shipping costs.
Historical analysis shows that El Niño typically causes only periodic supply disruptions, with a less persistent impact than that seen in agricultural commodities. During the super El Niño event of 2015–2016, extreme rainfall led to reduced copper production in Chile; total copper output for 2016 fell by 3.9% year-on-year, representing a loss of approximately 218,000 tonnes of metal. Of this, only 90,000 to 120,000 tonnes were directly attributable to climate factors.
Many institutions argue that El Niño serves merely as an amplifier for existing supply-demand imbalances rather than the primary driver of market trends. Localized production stoppages are only likely to push up copper prices when inventories are low and downstream demand remains resilient; if global demand weakens, weather-related issues will likely result in only a short-term price premium. In the medium to long term, copper prices will continue to be determined by the macroeconomic environment and downstream consumption. (Source: Shanghai Securities News)

This business plan report covers what capacity to target, which raw materials to secure, what machinery and site conditions are required, how capital and operating costs break down, and what profitability and regulatory factors determine commercial viability for a copper ingot manufacturing plant. It draws on IMARC Group's Copper Ingot Manufacturing Plant Project Report 2026, which benchmarks a facility with an annual production capacity of 10,000-30,000 tons.
Request Sample: https://www.imarcgroup.com/copper-ingot-manufacturing-plant-project-report/requestsample
Minimum Cost Required to Set Up a Copper Ingot Manufacturing Plant:
The minimum capital required to enter copper ingot manufacturing varies with plant scale and the degree of refining involved. Based on external industry benchmarking for copper remelting and secondary smelting facilities, a plant at the lower end of the report's 10,000-30,000 tons per year range needs roughly USD 8 million as an entry point, while small remelting units can start lower and large integrated smelting and refining complexes run well into the tens of millions.
Cost Breakdown by Plant Scale:
Small-Scale Copper Ingot Plant ($2M-$6M / ₹17Cr-₹50Cr): Focuses on melting clean copper scrap or cathode, basic refining, ingot casting, and packaging, generally using induction furnaces and moderate-capacity casting equipment, for volumes below the report's benchmark capacity.
Mid-Sized Copper Ingot Plant ($8M-$25M / ₹66Cr-₹208Cr): Aligned with the report's 10,000-30,000 tons per year capacity. 1. Why Copper Ingot Manufacturing Matters in 2026:
Copper ingots sit at the center of the global electrification push. Formed by casting molten copper into bars or blocks, they are the primary raw material for wires, cables, pipes, electrical components, and alloys. Copper's high thermal and electrical conductivity makes it essential across electronics, construction, automotive, and energy, and that dependence grows as grids expand and vehicles electrify. Demand is being pulled from two directions: infrastructure and electrical buildout, and the shift toward cleaner energy technologies.
Supply-side momentum and sustainability add to the case. The report notes that Canada's copper production rose 6.2%, from 484,552 tonnes in 2023 to 514,582 tonnes in 2024, expanding the supply of raw copper available for ingot production. Copper's recyclability also supports circular economy goals, and recycled copper makes up a significant portion of ingot production.
Why Invest in Copper Ingot Manufacturing?
Three factors make copper ingot manufacturing a comparatively attractive metals investment:
• Increasing demand for electrical products: Rising demand for electrical products, renewable energy, and electric vehicles is lifting the need for high-quality copper ingots, which feed wires, batteries, and motors.
• Growth of renewable energy technologies: The expansion of solar and wind markets boosts copper demand, as copper is widely used in electrical wiring, connectors, and solar panels.
• Recycling and sustainability trends: The focus on circular economies has increased the use of recycled copper, giving ingot producers access to scrap-based feedstock and a sustainability advantage.
Regional Insights:
Copper ingot demand is not uniform - it is shaped by each region's manufacturing base, power and electronics industries, and access to copper supply:
• Asia Pacific (China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, Philippines, Singapore): The largest regional market, holding 57.8% of the global copper ingot market according to the report, supported by dense wire, cable, and electronics manufacturing and rapid infrastructure and power-grid expansion.
• North America (U.S., Canada, Mexico): Holds roughly 19.6% of the global market, backed by electrical and automotive demand, grid and EV investment, and domestic copper supply growth such as Canada's rising output.
• Europe (Germany, U.K., France, Italy, Spain, Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Switzerland): Accounts for roughly 17.2% of the global market, driven by renewable energy deployment, electrification of transport, and a strong secondary copper and recycling industry.
• Latin America (Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, Colombia, Chile, Peru, Paraguay, Uruguay, Ecuador): Holds roughly 9.3% of the market and is a major copper ore producing region, though downstream ingot processing remains underdeveloped, creating room for value-added capacity.
• Middle East & Africa (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Israel, Egypt, South Africa, Nigeria, Morocco, Algeria, Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Ghana): Growing construction, power-infrastructure, and industrial diversification programs, alongside emerging local metals processing and recycling investments.
2. What is Copper Ingot and Where is It Used:
Copper ingots are solidified masses of molten copper formed in molds, typically as bars or blocks. They are produced by melting and refining copper ore or scrap to remove impurities, followed by casting, and they serve as the primary raw material for copper-based products. Their application footprint spans several industries:
• Electrical and electronics: Wires, cables, and electrical components such as conductors and transformers.
• Construction: Plumbing pipes, roofing, HVAC systems, and wiring.
• Automotive: Components for electric vehicles, batteries, radiators, and brakes.
• Energy and power generation: Solar panels, wind turbines, and transformers that rely on copper's conductivity.
• Aerospace: Aircraft electrical, brake, and fuel systems, where copper's strength and conductivity under extreme conditions matter.
This diversified end-use base is part of what supports steady demand even as individual sectors move through their own cycles.
3. Copper Ingot Manufacturing Process:
Copper ingot manufacturing follows a defined sequence of unit operations:
• Raw material sourcing - procurement of copper scrap or cathode and refining agents.
• Smelting and melting - feedstock is heated in furnaces to produce molten copper.
• Refining - impurities are removed to reach the required copper purity.
• Casting - molten copper is poured into molds to form ingots.
• Cooling and solidification - cast ingots are cooled and solidified to their final form.
• Packing and distribution - finished ingots are packaged, stored, and transported to wire, cable, and product manufacturers.
A robust quality assurance system should run in parallel with these stages, using technical tests and monitoring to confirm purity and consistency, with SOPs and documentation maintained for traceability and regulatory compliance.
4. Raw Materials and Sourcing:
Reliable feedstock supply is the single most important operating input for a copper ingot plant, given that raw materials account for 80-90% of operating expenses. Core raw material and process inputs include:
• Copper scrap (primary feedstock)
• Copper cathode (primary feedstock)
• Refining agents
• Packaging materials for finished ingots
Sourcing strategy should prioritize suppliers close to the plant to minimize transportation costs, alongside long-term contracts that stabilize pricing and secure supply continuity. Supply chain and sustainability risk should be assessed as part of supplier selection, since copper price volatility flows directly into margin.

Key equipment categories for a copper ingot manufacturing plant include:

articles.full_text:
Highlights
- BHP Group (ASX:BHP) reported lower copper output in 1QFY27 following maintenance, grade changes and disruptions.
- Western Australia Iron Ore recorded mine and port performance records in the September 2026 quarter.
- FY26 underlying EBITDA reached approximately USD 33bn, while attributable profit totalled USD 9.8bn.
- Jansen Stage 1 was 87% complete in October, with first potash production targeted for mid-2027.
BHP Group (ASX:BHP) produces copper, iron ore and steelmaking coal across major mining operations in Australia and the Americas, while developing a potash business in Canada. Its October operating review outlined lower first-quarter copper production, record activity across parts of its Western Australian iron ore network and further progress at Jansen. On 26 October 2026, BHP Group (ASX:BHP) was quoted at AUD 55.625, up 1.05% during the trading session. The company’s FY26 financial results and September-quarter disclosures provide the latest context for production, earnings and capital expenditure.
Company Business
BHP Group (ASX:BHP) operates Western Australia Iron Ore (WAIO) in the Pilbara and has copper interests that include Escondida in Chile and Copper South Australia. Its portfolio also comprises steelmaking coal operations in Queensland and other interests in the Americas. The company sells raw materials used in steel production, electrical equipment, construction and industrial activity.
The development portfolio includes copper processing capacity at Escondida, options across South Australia and the Americas, and the Jansen potash project in Saskatchewan, Canada. Potash would broaden the group’s commodity mix beyond its established mining operations. Production, processing capacity, rail logistics and port infrastructure determine how much material reaches customers.
Recent Development
In its 20 October 2026 operational review, BHP Group (ASX:BHP) reported reduced copper production in 1QFY27, citing planned lower ore grades, scheduled maintenance, severe weather in Chile, safety stoppages and a conveyor failure at Carrapateena. The company reported records at WAIO’s mine and port, while BMA and NSW Energy Coal production rose compared with the corresponding quarter a year earlier.
The group also said Jansen Stage 1 had reached 87% completion, compared with 84% at its August FY26 results announcement. First production remained scheduled for mid-2027. BHP continued work on its proposed new Escondida concentrator and copper growth options in South Australia and the Americas. The October review identified higher energy and freight costs, geopolitical tensions and trade uncertainty as factors affecting mining operations and markets.
Financial Performance and Sector Context
For FY26, BHP Group (ASX:BHP) reported approximately USD 33bn in underlying EBITDA, an increase of 27% from the preceding financial year, according to its annual reporting. Attributable profit was USD 9.8bn and free cash flow reached USD 9.8bn, up 83%. Net debt ended the period below USD 9bn. Capital expenditure and exploration spending totalled USD 10.3bn.
Copper generated approximately USD 18bn of underlying EBITDA, accounting for more than half of the group total for the first time. BHP produced about 2mn tonnes of copper for the second consecutive financial year and reported record WAIO production and shipments. Its FY26 results also recorded lower average unit costs across major assets despite inflation, diesel-price increases and supply-chain pressures.
Copper market conditions reflect industrial electrification, grid spending and physical supply constraints, while iron ore demand remains linked to steel production. BHP reported that copper prices in the September quarter were around 50% higher than a year earlier. Commodity prices may influence realised revenue even when production volumes move in the opposite direction.
Risks to Consider
BHP Group (ASX:BHP) remains exposed to fluctuations in copper, iron ore and coal prices, changing steel demand, operating costs and foreign exchange. Lower ore grades, weather disruptions and equipment reliability can affect output. Capital projects require approvals, construction execution and spending discipline. Workplace safety remains a material operational issue following fatalities disclosed in the October quarter review, with investigations underway. Higher freight and energy costs may also affect margins.
What to Watch Next
Key monitoring points for BHP Group (ASX:BHP) include copper output recovery after 1QFY27 interruptions, WAIO shipments, the progress of Escondida processing plans and the Jansen construction schedule. The next operating review is scheduled for January 2027, followed by half-year results in February. BHP has indicated medium-term average annual capital expenditure of approximately USD 11bn, with more than half intended for copper growth projects.
Key Insights
BHP’s September-quarter update combined operational records in iron ore with lower copper output and continued spending on copper and potash expansion. FY26 earnings and cash generation provide the financial backdrop for these investments. Production trends, project completion, commodity prices and the cost of execution will remain central to its subsequent updates.

articles.full_text:
Codelco
State-owned
Expectations for copper consumption tied to AI data centers, along with projections of a demand surge in India, may be overstated, experts cautioned at the Triland Global Metals Outlook hosted by Triland Metals during LME Week, according to Platts. Speaking at the conference, Bruce Alway, director of metals research at London Stock Exchange Group Data & Analytics, pointed to a calculation error in estimates of data center copper usage that has inflated the perceived needs of those facilities.
On India, Alway argued that even at its peak the country may not consume the metal at China's historic rate, citing lower metal intensity in modern infrastructure and greater circularity. He also noted that technologies such as fiber optics reduce copper usage inside data centers.
Alway said China, the world's largest market, is slowing, as declines in construction and home appliances are not offset by expanding power grid and electrical demand. He noted that China's electronics, AI and battery manufacturing index reached an all-time peak of 59.7 points in August, while the construction index stood at 42.9, far below its historic peak. China's yearly copper consumption growth is projected to fall to 1%-1.5% toward 2030, a deceleration that could turn the country into a net copper exporter.
Projected supply deficits have pushed copper prices to record highs above levels reflecting underlying demand, but soaring costs are forcing even booming sectors to scale back purchasing, according to the panel. Alway said the state-run power grid sector is highly price-sensitive, and projects mandated by the government are being delayed to await lower copper prices.
Tanja Winter, executive director of German copper recycling company Aurubis, told the panel that when copper prices peaked above $14,000 per metric ton, customers immediately stopped fulfilling orders. She said adjusting to price spikes requires substantial working capital and burdens cash flow, compounded by payment terms in which customers often wait 60, 80 or 120 days to be paid, and that even large original equipment manufacturers have slowed payment frequencies to once a month.
Winter said the debate over copper-to-aluminum substitution has peaked but is now driven by flawed logic. Five years ago substitution occurred naturally when the copper-to-aluminum price ratio hit 3:1, while today copper is almost 4.8 times more expensive than aluminum. She said anxiety over scarcity has triggered unnecessary panic-buying, and that fear of shortages is a poor reason to switch, especially for high-precision components. She added that Germany's automotive industry is under financial pressure and that carmakers are pivoting to aluminum under the guise of sustainability, though aluminum is often a poor choice on technical, lifetime performance and functional grounds.
Alway pointed to aluminum substitution in air conditioning, where manufacturers are designing high-efficiency units with thin-walled aluminum tubes instead of copper. He said aluminum has about 60% of copper's electrical conductivity, requiring thicker wires, but the price gap is already significant, and that substitution would skyrocket if the copper-aluminum price ratio stretched to 6:1-7:1. He said the era of high copper intensity from when prices were much lower is gone.
Alway noted that the copper concentrate market is emerging from a period of disruptions from May 2025 to August 2026, including rare snow in the Atacama Desert from El Nino, a mud flood at Grasberg and seismic activity at Kamoa-Kakula that halted major mines. Kamila Slupek, secretary general at the International Copper Study Group, told the panel that this year's growth in copper mine production is concentrated in Mongolia, Indonesia and Russia, with China expanding its Yulong mine and Peru's Antamina mine expected to deliver slightly higher output. She said traditional concentrate supplies will decline as production in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Indonesia faces constraints, with Kamoa-Kakula and Grasberg not yet fully recovered.
Although the industry does not anticipate sizable supply shocks in 2027, concentrate treatment charges remain deeply negative. Winter said smelters must pay miners $1,500 per ton of refined copper, which she described as unhealthy. She said Western smelters narrowly avoid closures thanks to elevated prices for co-products such as precious metals and sulfuric acid, but those revenue drivers are independent of copper and could evaporate at any moment.
Alway said Chinese smelters are cushioned because, through joint ventures, China owns 25% of global copper mine supply, including two-thirds of Africa's mining operations. He said China is increasing imports from its own overseas assets such as the Mirador mine in Ecuador and Oyu Tolgoi in Mongolia, and that its relationships with Chile and Peru, which provide 60% of its copper imports, remain solid, with brownfield expansions ensuring China maintains its smelting dominance.
Intense competition for concentrate has put secondary feedstocks in the spotlight, with retaining scrap metal domestically in Europe becoming a strategy partly encouraged by major OEMs pressuring local suppliers to deliver higher-recycled-content metals. Winter said cooperation with OEMs should be more reciprocal, noting that they request higher recycling rates for marketing purposes but sell their own factory scrap to traders that ship it to China.
Higher copper prices should make urban mining more economically viable, and dedicated projects are picking up in France and Germany, but copper recycling faces the same economic traps as the EV battery black mass sector, where two-thirds of planned recycling plants are shutting down due to processing complexity. The panel added that other inflationary pressures and scrap export bans are not helping the economics of scrap collection.
